Title: 3 Everyday Foods That Make Body Odor Worse

Description:
Notice people take a small step back mid-conversation, even hours after your shower? Body odor forms when food compounds are released through sweat and breath - and garlic, red meat, and alcohol can all push that further than you'd expect.

Each one has a simple fix that doesn't mean giving it up for good - just a change in how you cook or pair it.

Watch to find out why, and what to do instead.

platforms.title: Body Odor That Deodorant Can't Fix: 3 Foods Working Against You
platforms.meta_description: Reapplying deodorant but the smell keeps coming back? Garlic, red meat, and alcohol can affect body odor for hours — here's what actually helps.
platforms.body_html:
You've reapplied deodorant twice today, but the smell is back within hours anyway? Deodorant only masks what's on the surface — some everyday foods release odor-causing compounds through sweat and breath for hours after you eat them, and three in particular come up again and again: garlic and onion, red meat, and alcohol. Here's how each one actually affects body odor, and what tends to help more than another swipe of deodorant.

Sweat Itself Barely Smells

Fresh sweat is mostly water, and its job is cooling. The smell appears afterwards, when bacteria living on the skin break down the substances sweat carries with it. That reaction happens on the skin, not inside the gland, which is why a shower buys you a few hours rather than a whole day. It also explains why the smell concentrates in a few places: the armpits and groin have a different type of gland that switches on at puberty. The NHS lists what turns the volume up — exercise, hot weather, hormonal changes, being overweight — and notes the cause is often simply unknown. This is chemistry rather than carelessness, and what leaves your body through the skin is the raw material bacteria work with.

Garlic and Onion: Sulfur That Doesn't Quit

Garlic and onion contain allicin, which breaks down during digestion into volatile sulfur compounds like allyl methyl sulfide. These compounds enter the bloodstream and are released gradually over time — through the lungs as garlic breath, but also through the skin, where they mix into sweat. Because the body clears them slowly, the smell can still be noticeable more than a day after eating, even after multiple showers.

Red Meat: A Slower Trip Through Digestion

Red meat, like beef, takes longer to digest than fish or poultry. That extra time in the gut gives bacteria more opportunity to break down proteins, producing additional sulfur-containing byproducts that are eventually released through sweat. In a small 2006 experiment published in Chemical Senses, researchers at Charles University in Prague had 17 men alternate two weeks on a meatless diet with two weeks eating a lot of red meat, then asked 30 women to smell the sweat samples: odor from the meatless period was rated more pleasant, more attractive, and less intense. The sample is small, but it points the same way as the mechanism above.

Alcohol: The Detour Through Acetic Acid

The liver breaks alcohol down in two steps — first into acetaldehyde, then into acetic acid, the same compound found in vinegar. Roughly 90% of the alcohol you drink follows this path, but a smaller portion leaves the body unchanged, or as an intermediate byproduct, through sweat and breath. That portion is what gives sweat its sour, slightly sharp edge the morning after drinking. There's a second effect stacked on top: the NHS advises people who sweat heavily to avoid drinking alcohol or eating spicy food, because both push sweat production up.

What Changes When You Cook Them Instead

  • Cook garlic and onion instead of eating them raw — heat breaks down some of the allicin before digestion even starts. A raw apple, fresh mint leaves, or lettuce eaten right after can also neutralize some of the remaining sulfur compounds, according to a Journal of Food Science study on the enzymes in these foods.
  • Swap red meat for fish or chicken breast now and then — these proteins digest faster, leaving gut bacteria less time to produce odor-causing byproducts.
  • Drink water alongside alcohol — this dilutes its concentration in the body and supports the liver's breakdown process, which can reduce the portion released through sweat.

The Basics the NHS Actually Names

The official self-care list is short and unglamorous. The NHS recommends washing your armpits, groin and feet at least twice a day with soap, drying thoroughly, using antiperspirants and deodorants, changing and washing clothes regularly, wearing natural fabrics such as cotton, wool and silk, and choosing moisture-wicking socks changed at least twice a day. Its two "don'ts" are the same two foods this article started with: don't eat too much strong-smelling or spicy food, and don't drink too much alcohol. A pharmacist can also supply things without a prescription — stronger antiperspirants rather than plain deodorant, sweat shields to protect clothing, foot powders, and gentler soap substitutes if washing twice a day dries out your skin.

When It's Worth Seeing a Doctor

There is a line where self-care stops being the answer. The NHS suggests seeing a GP if body odor persists despite self-treatment and it's affecting your self-esteem, if you notice a change in how it usually smells, or if you suddenly begin to sweat much more than usual. For heavy sweating specifically, the prompts include symptoms lasting at least six months, happening at least once a week, interfering with daily activities, night sweats, or a family history. Conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease and liver disease can play a role, and some medicines — antidepressants among them — list sweating as a side effect. Never stop a prescribed medicine or change the dose on your own; raise it with the prescriber, who can judge whether an alternative exists.

Cooking Garlic Beats Buying Stronger Deodorant

If you take one thing from all of this, make it the cooking step: heat disarms part of the allicin before it ever reaches your bloodstream, which is the single change that acts on the cause rather than the surface. This article is for general information only and isn't medical advice, so if the smell persists despite these changes or shows up suddenly and strongly, it's worth checking with a doctor.
